transcript.heading: News Report One (American Female)
paras: A new study has found that reading for just 20 minutes a day can significantly reduce stress levels and improve mental well-being, according to researchers at the University of Sussex. The study measured the heart rate and muscle tension of participants before and after reading, and found that reading reduced stress by up to 68 percent, making it more effective than listening to music, walking, or drinking tea. Researchers say that reading requires concentration, which distracts the mind from daily worries and tensions, and that the immersive nature of reading helps the body relax. The study found that even reading for just a few minutes can have a noticeable effect, and that the type of reading material doesn't matter much—both fiction and non-fiction can be beneficial.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What did the University of Sussex study find about reading?
2. Why does reading reduce stress according to researchers?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: The city of Vancouver has launched an innovative program called "Play Streets," where residential streets are temporarily closed to traffic so that children can play safely outside. The program allows neighborhoods to apply to close their street for a few hours on weekends or after school, creating safe spaces for children to ride bikes, play games, and socialize. The goal is to encourage children to be more physically active, reduce screen time, and build stronger community connections. Vancouver is the first major Canadian city to implement such a program on a large scale. Supporters say that Play Streets help create safer, more livable neighborhoods and give children the kind of free, unstructured play that was common in previous generations.

4. What is one goal of the program?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Male)
paras: A study by researchers at Princeton University has found that taking notes by hand is more effective for learning and retention than typing notes on a laptop. The study followed hundreds of college students and found that those who took notes by hand performed better on conceptual questions and had a deeper understanding of the material compared to those who typed their notes. Researchers say that when people type, they tend to transcribe lectures verbatim without processing the information, while handwriting is slower, which forces students to listen more carefully and summarize information in their own words. This process of summarization and processing leads to better understanding and retention. The study's authors suggest that students consider taking notes by hand, at least for some classes, to improve their learning.

6. What did the Princeton study find about note-taking?
7. Why is handwriting more effective according to researchers?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Tom): Hey Sarah, I just got back from Japan! It was an amazing trip.
Woman (Sarah): Oh, how exciting! I've always wanted to go to Japan. How was it?
Man: It was incredible. I spent two weeks there, visiting Tokyo, Kyoto, and Osaka. There's so much to see and do, and the culture is fascinating.
Woman: That sounds amazing. What was your favorite part?

Man: Hmm, that's hard to say. I really loved Tokyo—it's such an exciting city, so modern and vibrant, but also with these beautiful traditional temples and gardens mixed in. But Kyoto was also amazing—so many historic temples and shrines, and the atmosphere is so peaceful.
Woman: I've seen pictures of Kyoto. It looks beautiful. Did you do any traditional activities?

Man: Yeah! I took a tea ceremony class in Kyoto, which was really interesting. And I wore a kimono for a day and walked around the old district. It was a lot of fun, though the kimono was a bit uncomfortable.
Woman: Ha, I can imagine. What about the food? I've heard Japanese food is amazing.

Man: Oh, the food was incredible! I ate so much good food—sushi, ramen, tempura, okonomiyaki... everything was delicious. And it's not just the fancy restaurants—even the cheap places and convenience store food was really good.
Woman: That's great to hear. I'm a vegetarian, though. Would I have trouble finding food?

Man: Hmm, that's a good question. Japanese food does use a lot of fish and meat, and even dishes that seem vegetarian often have fish sauce or bonito flakes. But there are vegetarian options, especially in bigger cities. There are Buddhist vegetarian restaurants called shojin ryori, which are amazing. And many places have tofu dishes. You just have to do a little research and ask.
Woman: Good to know. What about getting around? Is it easy to travel between cities?

Man: Super easy! The shinkansen, or bullet train, is amazing. It's fast, comfortable, and always on time. I took it from Tokyo to Kyoto, and it only took about two and a half hours. And within cities, the subway systems are really efficient, though they can be crowded during rush hour.
Woman: That sounds great. Was there anything you found surprising or difficult?

Man: Well, the language barrier was a bit challenging at times. Not many people speak English outside of the major tourist areas, so I had to use a translation app a lot. But people were really friendly and helpful, even when we couldn't communicate well. And the etiquette takes some getting used to—like taking off your shoes in certain places, not tipping, and being quiet on trains.
Woman: Yeah, I've heard about that. Do you have any tips for someone planning a trip?

Man: Definitely get a JR Pass if you're traveling between cities—it saves a lot of money on the bullet trains. And try to learn a few basic Japanese phrases—people really appreciate it. Also, don't overplan your itinerary—leave some time to just wander and explore. Some of my best experiences were the unplanned ones.
Woman: Those are great tips. I'm even more excited to go now. Thanks for sharing, Tom!
Man: No problem! You'll love it. Let me know if you have more questions when you start planning.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What traditional activity did Tom do in Kyoto?
10. What does Tom say about vegetarian food in Japan?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Emma): Hey Liam, how's your university application going? Have you started your personal statement yet?
Man (Liam): Ugh, don't even get me started. I've been staring at a blank document for weeks. I have no idea what to write.
Woman: I know how you feel—personal statements are so hard. But you have to start somewhere. What are you planning to study?
Man: I want to study history. I've always loved history, especially modern European history. But how do I make that sound interesting in a personal statement?

Woman: Well, first of all, you need to show your passion for the subject. Admissions officers want to see that you genuinely love the subject, not just that you're good at it. What made you interested in history?

Man: Hmm, I think it started when I was a kid and my grandparents would tell me stories about their lives during the war. It made me realize that history isn't just about dates and facts in a textbook—it's about real people and their lives.
Woman: That's a great starting point! You could write about that—how your grandparents' stories sparked your interest in history. That's personal and shows where your passion comes from.
Man: Yeah, that's a good idea. But what else should I include? I know I need to show that I've done extra reading or activities related to the subject.
Woman: Definitely. Admissions officers want to see that you're engaged with the subject beyond the classroom. Have you read any history books outside of school? Or done any related activities?

Man: Well, I read a lot of history books in my free time. Last year I read a book about the Cold War that was really interesting. And I volunteer at a local museum on weekends, helping with exhibits and giving tours to visitors.

Woman: That's perfect! Both of those are great to include. The museum volunteering shows that you're practically engaged with history, not just theoretically. And you can mention the book and what you learned from it.
Man: Yeah, that makes sense. What about structure? How should I organize the personal statement?

Woman: A good structure is: start with what sparked your interest in the subject, then talk about your academic achievements and extra reading, then mention any relevant work experience or volunteering, and finally talk about your future goals and why you want to study at university.
Man: That's helpful. What about the opening? I always struggle with the first sentence.

Woman: Don't try to be too clever or dramatic. Just be honest and genuine. Start with something specific that shows your interest—like the story about your grandparents, or a specific moment when you realized you loved history. Avoid clichés like "I have always been passionate about history since I was a child."
Man: Ha, okay, I'll avoid that. How long should it be?

Woman: The maximum is 4,000 characters or 47 lines, whichever comes first. That's about 500-600 words. You want to be concise and make every word count. Don't repeat yourself or include irrelevant information.
Man: Got it. What about achievements? Should I list all my grades and awards?

Woman: No, your grades are already on your application. The personal statement is about your passion and engagement with the subject, not a list of achievements. You can mention relevant achievements, but only if you can explain what you learned from them or how they relate to your subject.
Man: That makes sense. I think I have a better idea of what to do now. Thanks, Emma. You've been a huge help.
Woman: No problem! And if you want, when you have a draft, I can look it over and give you feedback.
Man: Really? That would be amazing. Thank you so much.
Woman: Of course. Good luck with it! I'm sure it'll be great.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: The Great Wall of China is one of the most iconic structures in the world, stretching over 13,000 miles across northern China. It's often called the longest man-made structure ever built, and it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most popular tourist attractions in the world. But there are many myths and misconceptions about the Great Wall, and the real history is even more fascinating than the legends.

One of the most common myths is that the Great Wall is a single, continuous wall that's visible from space. In reality, the Great Wall isn't one wall at all—it's a series of walls, fortifications, and natural barriers that were built and rebuilt by different dynasties over more than 2,000 years. And despite the popular myth, the wall is not visible from the moon with the naked eye, and it's very difficult to see even from low Earth orbit.

The earliest sections of the wall were built during the Warring States period (476-221 BCE) by individual states to protect themselves from each other and from nomadic tribes. When the first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang, unified China in 221 BCE, he ordered the connection and extension of these walls to create a unified defense system against the Xiongnu nomads from the north. These early walls were mostly made of rammed earth and wood, and much of them has eroded away over time.

The most famous and best-preserved sections of the wall were built much later, during the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644 CE). The Ming Dynasty faced constant threats from the Mongols and other nomadic groups, so they invested heavily in building a massive, sophisticated defense system. The Ming walls were made of brick and stone, with watchtowers, barracks, fortresses, and signal towers placed at regular intervals. The wall was also an important economic and cultural tool, used to control trade, immigration, and taxation along the northern border.

Contrary to popular belief, the Great Wall wasn't always effective at keeping invaders out. While it worked well for small raids and as a deterrent, several major invasions succeeded in getting past the wall, either by finding weak points or by bribing the guards. The most famous example is the Manchu invasion in 1644, which led to the fall of the Ming Dynasty and the establishment of the Qing Dynasty.

Today, the Great Wall is a symbol of Chinese civilization and a testament to the ingenuity and perseverance of the Chinese people. Millions of tourists visit every year, but much of the wall is in poor condition, especially in remote areas. Conservation efforts are ongoing to protect and restore this remarkable historical monument for future generations.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: Color psychology is the study of how colors affect human behavior, emotions, and perceptions. While the field is still evolving and many claims are debated, research has shown that colors can have measurable effects on our mood, decisions, and even physical responses.

Different colors are often associated with different emotions and meanings, though these associations can vary by culture and personal experience. Warm colors—red, orange, and yellow—are generally associated with energy, warmth, and excitement. Red is particularly powerful: it can increase heart rate and blood pressure, create a sense of urgency, and grab attention. That's why red is often used in sales, clearance signs, and fast food branding. Orange is energetic and friendly, while yellow is cheerful and optimistic.

Cool colors—blue, green, and purple—tend to have a calming effect. Blue is one of the most popular colors worldwide and is often associated with trust, stability, and serenity. Many banks, tech companies, and healthcare organizations use blue in their branding to convey reliability and professionalism. Green is associated with nature, health, growth, and freshness, making it popular with environmental and organic brands. Purple is often linked to creativity, luxury, and spirituality.

But color psychology isn't just about branding and marketing. It's used in interior design to create specific moods in different spaces. For example, blue and green are often used in bedrooms because they're calming and promote sleep. Warm colors like yellow and orange are used in dining areas because they can stimulate appetite. Red is sometimes used in gyms because it can increase energy and motivation.

It's important to note that color associations aren't universal. Cultural differences play a big role: for example, white symbolizes purity and weddings in Western cultures but represents death and mourning in many Eastern cultures. Red means luck and happiness in China but can symbolize danger in Western contexts. Personal experiences also shape how we respond to colors—if you have positive memories associated with a certain color, you'll likely respond more positively to it.

While color psychology can be a useful tool, it's important not to overstate its effects. Colors influence our mood and behavior, but they're just one factor among many, and the effects are often subtle. Still, understanding how colors affect us can help us make more informed choices in everything from design to daily life.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Urban agriculture—the practice of growing, processing, and distributing food in or around urban areas—is a growing movement in cities around the world. As more people move to cities and become concerned about food sustainability, health, and community, urban agriculture offers a way to reconnect with food production and build stronger, more resilient communities.

Urban agriculture takes many forms. Community gardens are shared plots of land where neighbors grow food together. Rooftop gardens use otherwise unused space on top of buildings. Vertical farms are indoor facilities that grow crops in stacked layers under artificial light, using hydroponics or aeroponics instead of soil. Backyard gardens, balcony gardens, and even window boxes are all forms of urban agriculture. Some cities also have urban farms—larger operations that sell produce at farmers markets or to local restaurants.

One of the main benefits of urban agriculture is its positive environmental impact. Locally grown food doesn't need to be transported long distances, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and packaging waste. Plants and soil help absorb rainwater, reducing stormwater runoff and flooding. Green spaces also help reduce the urban heat island effect, where cities are significantly hotter than surrounding rural areas due to all the concrete and asphalt. And urban farms can help improve soil quality and biodiversity in cities.

Urban agriculture also improves food access and public health. In many low-income neighborhoods, fresh, healthy food is hard to find—these areas are often called "food deserts." Community gardens and urban farms can provide affordable, nutritious produce to residents who might otherwise rely on fast food and convenience stores. Gardening itself is also a form of physical activity, and studies show that people who garden tend to eat more fruits and vegetables.

The social benefits are equally important. Community gardens bring people together, creating spaces where neighbors can meet, share knowledge, and build relationships. They provide educational opportunities for children and adults to learn about where food comes from, nutrition, and environmental stewardship. And for many people, gardening is therapeutic—it reduces stress, provides a sense of purpose, and creates a tangible connection to the natural world.

Of course, urban agriculture faces challenges. Finding suitable land is often difficult in dense cities, and soil contamination can be a concern on former industrial sites. Water access, zoning regulations, and funding are also common hurdles. But despite these challenges, the urban agriculture movement continues to grow, driven by passionate individuals and communities who believe in the power of growing food locally.
